title: Pitch, octave, and pitch class
description: Retain the difference between pitch, octave, and pitch class, plus the guitar facts from this lesson.

cards.back: How high or low a note sounds. It corresponds to frequency, measured in hertz (Hz).
The distance between a pitch and the pitch with double its frequency (a 2:1 ratio). Different pitches, same letter name.
The name shared by every pitch that is a whole number of octaves apart. A is a class; A2, A3, and A4 are three pitches in that class.

cards.front: What does the class tell you, and what does the octave number tell you?
cards.back: The class tells you what note. The octave number tells you where (which pitch).

cards.front: Why is an octave defined by doubling frequency, not by adding a fixed number of hertz?
cards.back: Hearing is roughly logarithmic. 110→220 Hz sounds like the same step as 220→440 Hz, even though the second gap is twice as large in hertz.

cards.front: Does the same pitch class mean the same sound?
cards.back: No. E2 and E4 are clearly different pitches. They are the “same note” only in the naming system.

cards.front: What is the frequency of A4? Of A5? Of A3?
cards.back: A4 = 440 Hz. A5 = 880 Hz. A3 = 220 Hz. Each octave doubles or halves the frequency.

cards.front: Name the pitch class and approximate frequency of A2, A3, and A4.
cards.back: All are pitch class A. A2 ≈ 110 Hz, A3 ≈ 220 Hz, A4 ≈ 440 Hz.

cards.front: Name the pitch class of C3, C5, G2, and G4. Which of each pair is higher?
cards.back: Classes: C, C, G, G. Higher pitches: C5 over C3, G4 over G2.

cards.front: Name the open strings from 6 to 1, with octave numbers.
cards.back: E2, A2, D3, G3, B3, E4. Strings 6 and 1 are both E, two octaves (24 semitones) apart.

cards.front: Why does the 12th fret sound one octave above the open string?
cards.back: It sits at half the string’s vibrating length, which doubles the frequency. Open A2 → 12th-fret A3.

cards.front: Play open string 5 (A2), then string 5 fret 12 (A3). What changed, and what stayed the same?
cards.back: The pitch is higher (A3 vs A2). The pitch class is still A.

cards.front: Guitar music is usually written how, relative to sounding pitch?
cards.back: One octave higher than it sounds. A written E3 sounds as E2. Octave numbers in these lessons are sounding pitch (A4 = 440 Hz, middle C = C4).

cards.front: Using frets 0–5, where does E occur on strings 6, 4, 2, and 1?
cards.back: String 6 fret 0 (E2), string 4 fret 2 (E3), string 2 fret 5 (E4), string 1 fret 0 (E4). The last two are the same pitch.

cards.front: “Which note is this?” vs “Which of those two Es is higher?” — which is pitch class, which is pitch?
cards.back: “Which note?” is pitch class. “Which E is higher?” is pitch. Chord and scale theory mostly ask the first; voicing and melody ask both.

cards.front: What does doubling a part an octave higher or lower do to the harmony?
cards.back: It thickens the sound without adding a new harmony. Scales and chords keep the same name across octaves.

cards.front: Why do E2 and E4 count as one pitch class but are not interchangeable in a part?
cards.back: They share a name, but they are different pitches (two octaves apart). Register matters for voicing, melody, and which string you choose.

cards.front: How can you check a sung octave above a note on string 6?
cards.back: Play two strings up and two frets higher (string 6 fret n to string 4 fret n+2). That shape is exactly one octave up.
